subject: 7A8829E6EC2442739DC33E5133C1D8EB
introduction: “The most despised of men in the sight of God are they who sit and beg.” Bahá’u’lláh made work a religious duty and begging unlawful, and in the same verses made the support of those who cannot work an obligation of the community and its institutions. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá adds that the idle by choice are not to be supported, and that dervishes who live on alms have mistaken laziness for holiness. Paul’s rule, “if any would not work, neither should he eat”, and his own tentmaking are the precedent; the gleanings of Leviticus are an old way of providing without begging. “Give to him that asketh thee” is the saying the readings seem to contradict.
questions: How do the readings distinguish those who cannot work from those who will not? Who is to make that judgment?
If one may not give to a beggar, what is one obliged to do instead?
Why would begging be thought to injure the dignity of the one who begs?

outside.why: The most despised are they who sit and beg. If any would not work, neither should he eat.
The same law that despises idleness commands the open hand: thou shalt not harden thine heart, nor shut thine hand from thy poor brother. The reading says both in one sentence. How do they fit?
Lazy people should not be assisted, or everyone would leave his work. Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise.

Begging is unlawful, and giving to the beggar forbidden. Jesus: give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away. What do the readings put in place of the coin given in the street?
The meaning of the verse: the community must provide for those unable. Let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.
Everyone is to engage in an occupation. Study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands.
Some are idle and scattered. Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings.
Persian Bahá’ís in poverty never complain nor ask. I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.
A time in the East when there was no mendicancy. Thou shalt not wholly reap the corners of thy field; thou shalt leave them for the poor and stranger.
The basest are they that yield no fruit. Thou wicked and slothful servant.
Some assume the character of dervishes as a pretext. Paul, because he was of the same craft, abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers.
God has created man noble. So God created man in his own image.
Abandoning frivolous conduct does not mean being sour-faced. Eat thy bread with joy; let thy garments be always white.

shortfall: Readings 6 and 11 concern festivals and pastimes, and three further quotations repeat the rule already given a companion.
